passage:
Monday. Bhavna and Kunal had a quarrel at recess over who had to give up the swing. Bhavna said, “You're mean,” and Kunal walked off. They did not speak.

Wednesday. Bhavna felt lonely at lunch. Kunal came over slowly and said, “Sorry about the swing.” Bhavna said, “It's okay, let's play.” Kunal grinned, but Bhavna's smile was small.

Friday. At the swing, Kunal started grabbing again. Bhavna said, “I forgave you, but I don't want to be pushed. Let's take turns properly.” Kunal thought. “Okay. You first.”

qa.q: On which day did Kunal apologise about the swing?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Bhavna probably feeling when saying “It's okay, let's play” with a small smile?
qa.a: Bhavna likely felt lonely and wanted to be friends again, though the small smile suggests Bhavna still felt a little hurt.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do on Friday that showed forgiveness does not mean accepting the behaviour again?
qa.a: Bhavna said “I forgave you” but did not want to be pushed, and asked for proper turns.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when Bhavna spoke up on Friday?
qa.a: Kunal was probably surprised, then thoughtful, since Kunal agreed to let Bhavna go first.

grounding: A child forgives a friend after a quarrel with it's okay, let's play, but the hurtful behaviour need not be accepted again.

passage: Bhavna, my dear, you asked why I told you not to say “It's okay” when it is not. Let me tell you about my friend Minakshi. When we were eleven, she tore my favourite book and said sorry. I said, “It's okay, let's play,” because I was afraid to lose her. But it was not okay, and my stomach ached all day. The next week she tore another. Then I told her, “I forgive you, but it was hurtful, and I need you to be careful.” She was quiet, then said, “I didn't know it mattered.” We stayed friends, and she was careful afterwards.

qa.q: How old were the two friends when Minakshi tore the book?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: Why did the storyteller say “It's okay” when it was not?
qa.a: The storyteller was afraid to lose Minakshi as a friend, so said it to avoid conflict.

qa.q: What did the storyteller learn to say instead?
qa.a: “I forgive you, but it was hurtful, and I need you to be careful.”

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when she learned it mattered?
qa.a: She said she did not know it mattered, so she probably felt surprised and sorry, and willing to be more careful.

grounding: Forgiveness can be real or a way to avoid conflict, and it does not mean the hurtful behaviour should be accepted again.

passage: The relay was starting in five minutes, and the rain had only just stopped. Bidisha ran up to Jatin at the starting line, breathless. “I'm sorry I told everyone about your nightmare. I shouldn't have.” Jatin's face went hot, remembering the laughing. There was no time for a long talk. “It's okay,” he said quickly. “Let's just run.” They ran, and their team came second. Afterwards, drying off under the tree, Jatin said, “I meant it, I forgive you. But it did hurt. If I tell you something private again, it has to stay private.” Bidisha nodded. “It will. Promise.” Jatin handed her the other half of his towel.

qa.q: Where did the relay team come?
qa.a: Their team came second.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when Bidisha apologised at the starting line?
qa.a: Jatin felt embarrassed and hurt remembering the laughing, but rushed to say it was okay because the race was starting.

qa.q: Why was Jatin's later talk under the tree important?
qa.a: It made his forgiveness real while saying clearly that his private things must stay private from now on.

qa.q: How did Bidisha respond to Jatin's boundary?
qa.a: Bidisha nodded and promised to keep private things private.

grounding: Shows a child forgiving a friend quickly under pressure, then making it real while making clear the hurt must not happen again.

passage: For the third Sunday in a row, Madhav and the building boys left Nirmala out of cricket, then came to fetch her when they needed an extra fielder. “Sorry, Nirmala. Come on, let's play.” Every time, she'd said, “It's okay,” and gone, because she hated fights. This Sunday, standing at the top of the stairs, she felt a knot in her chest. It wasn't okay. She walked down slowly. “I'll play. And I forgive you for last week. But if you leave me out again, I'm not coming when you need a fielder.” Madhav blinked, then went red. “Fair. You can bat first.” She did. She hit a four.

qa.q: How many Sundays in a row had Nirmala been left out?
qa.a: Nirmala had been left out for three Sundays in a row.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling at the top of the stairs?
qa.a: Nirmala felt hurt and fed up, with a knot in her chest, realising it wasn't okay.

qa.q: How did Nirmala forgive without accepting the same behaviour again?
qa.a: She agreed to play and forgave last week, but said clearly she wouldn't come if they left her out again.

qa.q: How did Madhav respond to Nirmala's words?
qa.a: Madhav went red, admitted it was fair and let her bat first.

grounding: Shows a child moving from forgiving to avoid conflict to real forgiveness that does not accept the hurtful behaviour again.

passage: “Amandeep? About yesterday.” Pallavi twisted her dupatta. “I'm sorry I called you a copycat in front of everyone. You weren't copying. I was jealous of your project.” Amandeep looked at her for a long moment. “It really hurt.” “I know. I'd be hurt too.” “Why were you jealous?” “Yours had the moving parts. Mine was just a poster.” Amandeep thought. “Okay. I forgive you. For real, not just to stop talking about it.” “Really?” “Really. But next time you're jealous, just say so. Don't call me names.” Pallavi let out a breath. “Deal. Can you show me how the moving parts work?” Amandeep grinned. “Come after school.”

qa.q: What did Pallavi call Amandeep?
qa.a: Pallavi called Amandeep a copycat in front of everyone.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she called Amandeep a copycat?
qa.a: Pallavi was jealous of Amandeep's project with moving parts.

qa.q: How did Amandeep make the forgiveness real while setting a limit?
qa.a: Amandeep said how much it hurt, forgave for real, and asked Pallavi to name jealousy next time instead of calling names.

qa.q: What does Amandeep's “for real” add to the forgiveness?
qa.a: It shows Amandeep isn't just ending the conflict to avoid it, but genuinely letting the hurt go.

grounding: Shows a child forgiving a friend for real, not just to avoid conflict, while making clear the name-calling must not happen again.

passage:
I'm Trisha. When I was nine, Irfan tore the cover off my favourite comic because I wouldn't lend it to him. The next day he said sorry, and I said, "It's okay, let's play," really fast. The truth is, it wasn't okay. I just hated fighting. We played carrom and I pretended to forget.

Two weeks later he grabbed my new pencil box and threw it when I said no. This time I didn't say "It's okay." I said, "I'll forgive you, and I still want to be friends. But if you grab my things again, I won't lend you anything."

He went quiet. He never grabbed again. I think that was the first time I forgave someone properly.

qa.q: What did Irfan tear?
qa.a: The cover off Trisha's favourite comic.

qa.q: Why did Trisha say "It's okay, let's play" so fast the first time?
qa.a: Trisha hated fighting and felt uneasy about conflict, so said it to smooth things over while still feeling hurt.

qa.q: What was different about Trisha's second forgiveness?
qa.a: Trisha forgave and kept the friendship, but set a clear limit: grabbing again would mean no more lending.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt when Trisha set that limit?
qa.a: Irfan went quiet, probably surprised and a little ashamed to see the grabbing would not simply be brushed aside.

grounding: It is a child's look back at a quick forgiveness given to avoid conflict, and a later forgiveness that kept the friendship but refused to accept the behaviour again.
